title: Can I Trust My Feelings About God?
excerpt: Feelings about God can be produced on demand, and some of the strongest have been mistaken. They are also part of what Scripture calls faith. Jeremiah 17:9, the Psalms and a treatise Jonathan Edwards published in 1746 each refuse both a faith that is only feeling and a faith that despises it.
body:
A man of forty still remembers a night at a summer camp when he was sixteen, when he knew beyond any argument that God was real and near, and he has never felt it that way since. Lately he has begun to wonder whether it was the music, the late hour and the crowd. A woman had what everyone around her called a peace about a decision, the decision went badly, and she no longer trusts anything she feels in prayer. A man brought up in a church where tears were treated as weakness has sung the same hymns for thirty years without feeling much of anything, and he has always assumed that was maturity. A young woman stood in a stadium at a concert last summer and felt exactly what she used to feel in church, and she has not been back to church since.

The skeptic says aloud what the young woman suspects. People of every religion report the presence of the divine, and their experiences point to different gods. The same rush can be produced by music, a crowd, the right lighting, fasting or lack of sleep, and the people who stage concerts and the people who plan services both know how. A feeling that can be manufactured on demand, he says, is evidence about the person who has it and about nothing else.

Most of that should be granted. Christians have produced feelings on purpose and then called them God, and a great many sincere people have mistaken their own longing for an answer. But the argument proves less than it seems to. That a feeling can be caused does not show what caused it, and an account of where a belief came from cannot settle whether the belief is true. The site's Honest Answer on [whether faith is just wishful thinking](/answers/is-faith-just-wishful-thinking) takes up that argument in its strongest form. This essay asks a different question: what place feelings have in knowing God at all, and how Scripture and the church have taught believers to test them.

## What the Bible Means by the Heart

A verse often quoted against religious feeling is Jeremiah 17:9: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" It is offered as proof that emotions cannot be trusted and that a believer should rely on reason instead. The verse says something harder than that.

In Hebrew the heart meant far more than the emotions. The Study Bible's note on [Deuteronomy 30](/study/bible/deuteronomy/30) calls it "the center of thinking, will, and decision," and in Proverbs the ESV prints "mind" where the King James Version had "heart": "Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool" (Proverbs 28:26). So Jeremiah is not setting feelings against thoughts. He is speaking of the whole inner life, including the reasoning that distrusts feelings.

The verse also stands between two pictures. Just before it, Jeremiah sets the man who "trusts in man and makes flesh his strength" (Jeremiah 17:5) against the one who trusts in the Lord, who is "like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream" (Jeremiah 17:8). The note on [Jeremiah 17](/study/bible/jeremiah/17) draws the lesson in one line: "Faith is not a feeling but where a person sends their roots: toward human strength or toward the LORD." Just after it comes the answer to the verse's own question: "I the Lord search the heart and test the mind" (Jeremiah 17:10). Jeremiah does not tell anyone to distrust his heart and trust his head. He says that no one can fully read his own inner life, and that God can. The Honest Answer quotes the verse and adds that it "includes the believing heart." It includes the doubting heart too.

And the prophets did not leave the heart where they found it. God promised through Jeremiah, "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33), and through Ezekiel, "I will give you a new heart" (Ezekiel 36:26). Scripture's remedy for a deceitful heart is not to stop having one.

## The Psalms Feel, and Argue

The Psalms are full of feeling, and they argue with it too. They command it: "Delight yourself in the Lord" (Psalm 37:4). They expect it: "in your presence there is fullness of joy" (Psalm 16:11). And they report it honestly when it goes the other way.

Psalm 73 is a plain case. Its writer tells how his feelings nearly undid him. "I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (Psalm 73:3), and envy made the world look as though faithfulness did not pay. He tried to reason his way out and found it "a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16-17). Looking back, he names what the bitterness had made of him: "I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you" (Psalm 73:22). The next verse is the turn of the whole psalm: "Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand" (Psalm 73:23).

Psalm 77 does the same with a darker feeling. "Has God forgotten to be gracious?" its writer asks (Psalm 77:9), and he does not soften the question. Then he does something on purpose: "I will remember the deeds of the Lord" (Psalm 77:11).

In both psalms the feeling is treated as a true report about the person praying, and not always a true report about God. Neither writer despises what he feels, and neither simply obeys it. He brings it into God's presence and measures it against what God has done. It is the oldest teaching the church has on the subject, and Israel sang it before the church did.

## Experience as Evidence

Can a feeling about God count as evidence for him? One careful answer came from William James, in the lectures he gave at Edinburgh in 1901 and 1902 and printed as *The Varieties of Religious Experience*. James took experiences of the divine seriously, and he drew a line. Such states, he wrote, "usually are, and have the right to be, absolutely authoritative over the individuals to whom they come." But "No authority emanates from them which should make it a duty for those who stand outside of them to accept their revelations uncritically."

The New Testament keeps something like that line. It speaks of an inward witness: "The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God" (Romans 8:16). It also tells believers, "do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God" (1 John 4:1), and it places even an angel's message under the gospel already preached (Galatians 1:8). And it does not rest the faith on anyone's experience. Paul handed on "as of first importance" a set of events: "that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). On this account experience is the believer's response to those events and a witness within him that they are for him. It was never meant to be the evidence that they happened. That is also the beginning of an answer to the skeptic's first point. If experiences in every religion point different ways, then experience alone cannot decide among them, and the creeds never asked it to.

John Wesley, who taught that the inward witness is real, opened his sermon on it with a warning: "How many have mistaken the voice of their own imagination, for this witness of the Spirit of God?" One of his tests was humility. A true witness, he argued, leaves a person gentler and easier to correct, and the false one does the reverse: "The stronger witness he imagines himself to have, the more overbearing is he to all around him."

The same caution applies to the sense of peace many Christians wait for before a decision. A strong inner sense can come from God, and it can come from the wish to have the decision made. The site's page [How do I know what God wants me to do?](/help/decisions) gives the plainest test: "an impression that contradicts Scripture isn't from him, however strong it feels." The essay on [whether God has a plan for a life](/writing/does-god-have-a-plan-for-my-life) sets out how Christians have weighed such impressions beyond that.

## Edwards and the Affections

The site's [history course](/theology/history/awakenings-and-enlightenment) calls the answer Jonathan Edwards gave in the 1740s "the most careful answer the church has ever given." Revival had come to the New England town where he was pastor, and the course tells how he defended it and then became "its examiner." In 1746 he published *A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections*. On its title page he set two verses from Leviticus: the fire from the Lord at which the people "shouted and fell on their Faces," and the fire two priests brought on their own, which the title page calls "strange Fire," and which killed them (Leviticus 9:24; 10:1-2). Real fire and false fire can look alike, and the book is an attempt to tell them apart.

Edwards stated his thesis in one line: "True Religion, in great Part, consists in holy Affections." He did not mean what most people now mean by feelings. The affections, he wrote, "are no other, than the more vigorous and sensible Exercises of the Inclination and Will of the Soul." He named them: love, desire, hope, joy and gratitude on one side, hatred, fear, anger and grief on the other, the soul either "cleaving to" what it sees or turning away from it. He set them apart from passions, which come suddenly and leave the mind "less in its own Command." He defended the affections against those who had grown suspicious of them, and in the same book he refused to let them vouch for themselves. "There are false Affections, and there are true."

The second part of the treatise is a list of things that prove nothing either way, and it is still startling to read. "'Tis no Sign one Way or the other, that religious Affections are very great, or raised very high." Nor is it a sign that they have great effects on the body, that they make people talk freely about religion, or that they arrive with verses of Scripture brought suddenly to mind. It is no sign, Edwards wrote, "that they make Persons that have them, exceeding confident that what they experience is divine." The height of a feeling, its effects on the body and the certainty it brings were the very things many of the revival's admirers had counted as proof, and he set every one of them aside.

What does count? Edwards gave twelve signs, and the last of them is the one anyone can watch: "Gracious and holy Affections have their Exercise and Fruit in Christian Practice." He called a holy life "the chief of all the Signs of Grace," both to others "and also to their own Consciences." A century and a half later William James summed up the book as "an elaborate working out" of one principle: "By their fruits ye shall know them, not by their roots."

## Two Opposite Errors

Edwards watched the churches around him swing between two mistakes. "Thus we easily, and naturally run from one Extreme to another," he wrote, of Christians who had first treated every high feeling as grace and then, burned by the results, decided that religion had little to do with feeling at all. Both errors are still with us.

The first makes faith a feeling. It plans worship to produce a moment and then names the moment God. It measures a believer's nearness to God by how warm he feels, and it reads any strong inner sense as a word from heaven. One of its sharpest critics was an unbeliever. In 1841 the philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach argued that if feeling is the way to God, feeling is the god: "If, for example, feeling is the essential organ of religion, the nature of God is nothing else than an expression of the nature of feeling." Such a faith, he went on, no longer needs its doctrines, since "if another object would excite the same emotions, it would be just as welcome." His preface says the chapter had in view, among others, Friedrich Schleiermacher, the theologian who, in the words of the site's history course, "taught Protestant theology to ground itself in religious feeling itself." Against a faith built on feeling alone, Feuerbach's argument is very hard to answer. Against the creeds it has less force, because they confess things that happened, and those were the things the apostles pointed to.

The second error despises feeling. It treats tears as weakness and joy as immaturity, and it imagines that a correct belief held coldly is the more grown-up faith. The history course sums up the case of Charles Chauncy, the leading voice among the revival's critics in Boston: "the passions are the lowest part of a man and the easiest to play." He was right about many of the dangers, and Edwards still refused his conclusion: "As there is no true Religion, where there is nothing else but Affection; so there is no true Religion where there is no religious Affection." Where there is "Heat without Light," Edwards wrote, there is nothing divine, and the same holds for "Light without Heat." The Gospels do not show a Lord who kept his feelings out of his faith. Jesus wept for his friend Lazarus (John 11:35), looked at hard-hearted men "with anger" (Mark 3:5), "rejoiced in the Holy Spirit" (Luke 10:21), and endured the cross "for the joy that was set before him" (Hebrews 12:2). The greatest commandment asks for love "with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength" (Mark 12:30). And Peter wrote to people who had never seen Jesus that they loved him and "rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory" (1 Peter 1:8).

We have committed both errors, often in the same church on different Sundays. The history course says that the quarrel of the 1740s taught America "that order and fire are opposites, and a Christian must choose." Scripture never asked anyone to choose.

## If You Feel Nothing

Some readers come to this question because they feel nothing at all, toward God or toward much else, and for them it is not an academic question. Nothing in this essay can tell anyone why that is, and it is not medical advice. The site's page on [numbness](/wisdom/numbness) says what can be said to anyone: "When grief or sadness lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise, and it is not a failure of faith." It adds, "If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today." And: "The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn." [Find Help](/help) is that page. The essay on [why God can feel so far away](/writing/why-does-god-feel-far-away) takes up the long dry seasons in prayer.

Two things in this essay belong to such a reader. The first is that the absence of a feeling is no more a ruling on a soul than its presence would be. The Study Bible's study of the Holy Spirit says that "the Spirit's presence does not depend on the strength of a person's feelings," and the page on numbness says it more simply: "you are not measured by what you can feel." The second is that Scripture speaks to this person by name. "Who among you fears the Lord and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the Lord and rely on his God" (Isaiah 50:10). The prophet does not tell him to make light. He tells him whom to lean on while it is dark.

The man who felt God at sixteen may never feel that night again, and the woman who trusted her peace has learned something true about her own heart. Neither of them has learned that God was absent. The man who has sung for thirty years without tears may have been more faithful than he knew, or he may have been taught to be ashamed of something God made. The young woman in the stadium is right that a feeling can be produced, and the psalmist who nearly lost his footing would not have argued with her. He did not get his footing back by feeling better. He went into the sanctuary and saw what his bitterness had hidden, and near the end of his psalm he set down a sentence that grants the worst about the heart and holds on to God anyway.

*"My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever."* (Psalm 73:26)

*"For whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything."* (1 John 3:20)
